q: What is the empirical value of the volume-effect / statistical-dependence parameter δ in Eq.(1) P+ = PB - PI + δ(1 - PB)PI, and does a single scalar δ actually fit modern cohort data across tumor sites and modalities?
basis: Brahme asserts δ ≈ 0.2 as clinically realistic (near l.693 / l.1028) but never fits it to a deposited cohort in this paper; C11 is 'asserted, not derived'. Our monotonicity check confirms only that P+ rises with δ, not that 0.2 is right. Whether δ should be site-, modality-, or fractionation-dependent is left entirely open. The value drives the peak P+ by ~5 percentage points across δ ∈ [0,1] in our smoke, so it is not a rounding-level concern.
next_steps: (a) Assemble a small public cohort of paired tumor-control and severe-normal-tissue-complication outcomes from released radiotherapy series (e.g. QUANTEC-style aggregates, MSK/NIH open datasets, EORTC/RTOG published tables). (b) Fit Eq.(1) jointly for δ alongside a Källman/Brahme (D50, γ) pair per (site, modality). Compare a single global δ vs. per-site δ vs. (site×modality) δ by AIC/BIC. (c) Test whether δ varies with fractionation regime (SBRT vs. conventional). (d) Publish the fit + residuals + posterior on δ.

q: Does the RHR (Repairable-Homologous-Recombination) survival model actually outperform the LQ model and Brahme's own RCR model on low-dose hypersensitivity (LDHS) data, once tested on external, held-out cell-survival curves?
basis: Claim C9 ('RHR > LQ for LDHS') is central to Brahme's synthesis but is asserted; parameters are not deposited here and live in refs [1-3, 23, 34, 45]. The parameter table for RHR (a, b, repair rates, NHEJ vs. HR partitioning) is missing from this paper. Our audit could not touch this claim.
next_steps: (a) Pull cell-survival curves from open repositories (PIDE, RaySearch community datasets, GDC) covering both LDHS-prone and non-LDHS lines. (b) Fit LQ, LQ-L, RCR, and RHR to each curve using a common optimizer; report AIC/BIC, cross-validated log-likelihood, and prediction on held-out low-dose (< 0.5 Gy) points. (c) Publish the fit + a portable Python implementation of RHR so downstream users can decide whether the extra parameters are earned.

q: Is there any modality (light ions He–B, photon SBRT, proton, or carbon) whose LET-driven γ_C degradation is quantitatively predicted by microdosimetric heterogeneity (σ_D / Ŭ) values equal to what Brahme reports in the Figure 15 tabular insert (γ_C ≈ 4 for n/C vs. 5–6 for photons/Li)?
basis: Claim C5 is the only quantitative modality-level claim in the paper; the underlying values live inside a rendered figure text-box that pdftotext cannot recover. Whether these specific γ_C values are reproducible from microdosimetric first principles (Kellerer–Rossi lineal-energy variance, ICRU-36 style specific-energy distributions) is unaudited. C5 not tested.
next_steps: (a) Re-parse paper.pdf with Marker or Nougat (GPU) to recover the Figure 15 tabular insert as machine-readable text. (b) For each modality (photon 6–18 MV, proton spread-out Bragg peak, He–B ions, C ion), compute σ_D / Ŭ using published PIDE/PSTAR/SRIM stopping-power tables and standard cell-size assumptions. (c) Propagate σ_D / Ŭ into γ_C via the Källman/Brahme formula γ_C ≈ γ_C,0 / √(1 + (σ_D/Ŭ)²). (d) Compare predicted γ_C per modality against Fig. 15 values; publish a mismatch report + a proposal for a corrected table if the mismatch is > 20%.

q: Can the BIOART / IVPA per-voxel D0,eff workflow (FDG-PET-CT before and after ≈18 Gy → voxel-wise effective-dose map) be reproduced on any open multi-timepoint PET-CT radiotherapy dataset, and does the resulting D0,eff map improve local control vs. standard planning when used as a boost target?
basis: Claim C12 is the paper's most concrete clinical proposal but is illustrated only qualitatively via Figure 11 for a single unnamed lung case; no images, no D0,eff map, no cohort. C12 not tested.
next_steps: (a) Identify open PET-CT datasets with mid-treatment re-imaging at ≈18 Gy (TCIA HN-PET, TCIA NSCLC-Radiogenomics, EORTC public releases). (b) Implement a per-voxel FDG-uptake-to-D0,eff mapping following Brahme's cited derivation; deposit the code under a permissive license. (c) Simulate a boost plan driven by D0,eff and compare to standard-of-care plans on the same anatomy using TCP/NTCP surrogates. (d) If any dataset has follow-up outcome, run a retrospective concordance study; else report the pipeline + reproducibility only.

q: How should LUCID (and any large paper-replication corpus) systematically detect and handle 'review / synthesis in predatory-adjacent venue' papers so that they are neither silently promoted as REPLICATED nor silently discarded, and so that their citation chain to primary work is preserved for downstream audit?
basis: This slot exposed a pipeline failure mode: the paper passed initial screening as 'candidate_curated' despite being (i) a single-author review, (ii) in a Gavin Publishers venue widely flagged predatory, and (iii) containing zero primary artifact. It was audited, tagged REPLICATED (formalism-only), then retiered to NO-GO on 2026-06-25. This is expensive if it happens across a 100-slot corpus, and the current pipeline provides no upstream signal.
next_steps: (a) Add a pre-audit venue-quality check: compare journal against Beall-successor lists (e.g. Cabells Predatory Reports, DOAJ removal list, Kscien blacklist) and flag any hit before subagent time is spent. (b) Add a static PDF-content check: number of Methods-section pages, presence of a Data Availability statement, presence of any parameter table with > 5 rows; require at least one non-null of these to pass to full audit. (c) For any paper that passes venue+content check but is later verdict-flipped to NO-GO, log the delta so the pre-audit gate can be tuned. (d) For legitimate reviews (well-cited synthesis in reputable venues), route them to a distinct 'REVIEW_AUDIT' track that captures the citation-graph and reachable-primary-refs coverage instead of forcing a REPLICATED verdict. (e) Publish the gate rules as a small standalone package so other paper-replication projects can adopt them.
